title: Property Management Website Builder: 7 Options, Real Limits
html:
A property management website builder is either a stand-alone tool you pair with your software, or a site that comes inside your management platform. Stand-alone builders cost a few dollars a month. Platforms charge per unit. Either way, a managed website is the third path when you want it built for you. Published prices in this guide run from $4 a month to $2.50 per unit.

A property management website builder has to do two jobs that pull in opposite directions. It must win owners who might hire you and serve tenants who already rent from you. Owners compare managers on a phone before they call. Tenants want to pay rent, send a request and find a listing. One site rarely does both well without planning.

This guide covers seven options in two groups. Three are stand-alone builders, three are property management platforms that list a website or site feature, and one is a free map listing. Each gets the price its vendor publishes and one real limit, so you can see what you give up with every choice.

Which stand-alone website builders suit a property manager?

Wix, Squarespace and WordPress.com all let a property management company launch a site without a developer. They differ in how they show prices and what they limit.

The cheapest option is not always the right one. WordPress.com Personal costs $48 a year on a 12-month term, against $108 billed monthly, so the commitment saves $60. Wix Light costs about $213 for a year paid in full. Neither includes rent collection or tenant portals.

Property management sites need pages most small business sites skip. Plan a page for owners with a clear form, a page for each service area, a listings page and links to the tenant portal. Check that any builder you pick lets you add and edit those pages without a developer.

What property management software includes a website?

DoorLoop, Buildium and Rentvine are management platforms, not site builders. Their pages list a website or marketing site as part of the offering, and they charge in different ways.

  • DoorLoop: lists DoorLoop One at $2.50 per unit per month, Connect at $4.00 and Multiply at $5.00. The page marks a company website and a tenant portal as included. Limit: minimum spend and units apply to all plans, and you must contact sales for details.
  • Buildium: lists Essential from $65 a month, Growth from $202 and Premium from $420. Marketing Website and Resident Portal appear as features. Limit: the page does not show which plans include the website, so confirm with Buildium.
  • Rentvine: lists a rate as low as $1.50 per active unit, with no plan names. Smartsites powered by PMW appears as a feature. Limit: the page does not say whether the site is in the base price, and the one-time setup fee is not published.

Per-unit pricing scales with your portfolio. A manager with 60 units pays about $150 a month at DoorLoop One's starting rate, before any minimums. At Rentvine's lowest listed rate, 60 units would be $90 a month.

DoorLoop's page says the rate drops to $1.50 per unit above 100 units. It does not say whether the drop applies to every unit or only the extras. Ask for the exact math in writing before you assume a lower bill at 150 units.

Is a website inside your management software enough?

A website inside your management software is enough for tenants, but often not for winning owners. Platform sites usually share a template and a structure, and owner searches reward original content.

Ask five questions before you rely on one. Who owns the domain? Can you move the site if you change software? Can you edit page titles and descriptions? Can you add original pages for each city you serve? Can you install analytics?

Many managers keep both. The platform site handles the tenant side at a subdomain or a linked page, and a separate marketing site wins owners. That split avoids lock-in and gives each audience its own page structure.

Owner acquisition also depends on the search side. That is a managed build, not a template you edit yourself. It costs more than any builder here.

Content matters more than the template. A page that explains your fees and the areas you cover gives an owner a reason to call. So does a page on how you screen tenants and report to owners. A generic home page with a stock photo does not. Whichever tool you pick, budget time to write those pages yourself or hire help. Update them whenever your fees or service areas change.

Speed and mobile layout matter too. Owners often search from a phone between showings. Load your finished site on a phone and tap through the owner page, the listings page and the contact form before you launch. Fix anything that takes more than a few seconds to load.

What free tool puts a property manager on the map?

Google Business Profile is the free listing that shows a property management company in Google Maps when an owner searches for a manager nearby. Google states that you can add or claim your business at no charge.

  • Google Business Profile: shows your name, service area, phone number, hours and reviews. Limit: it only helps when the address is accurate and the profile gets fresh photos, posts and review replies.

Owners read reviews from both owners and tenants, so respond to every one. It pairs with property management SEO for owner-intent searches.

OptionTypePublished priceReal limit
WixStand-alone builder$17.77 to $39.77 a month, paid yearlyFree domain voucher is one year
SquarespaceStand-alone builderShown in Thai baht on the page readPrices unlabeled
WordPress.comStand-alone builder$4 to $45 a month, billed every 12 monthsNo custom domain on free plan
DoorLoopPlatform with site$2.50 to $5.00 per unit a monthMinimum spend applies
BuildiumPlatform with site feature$65 to $420 a monthPlan coverage unclear
RentvinePlatform with site featureAs low as $1.50 per unitSetup fee not published
Google Business ProfileMap listingFreeNeeds steady upkeep

How much does a property management website cost in practice?

A 60-unit manager has several honest options. A stand-alone builder such as WordPress.com Personal costs $4 to $9 a month, plus your own time. A platform such as DoorLoop costs about $150 a month at the starting rate, but covers far more than a website.

Compare like with like. The platform price pays for accounting, leasing and a tenant portal as well as a site. The builder price pays only for the site. If you already pay for software, the website is a small extra. If you do not, the platform is the larger decision.

Time is the other cost. A builder site needs someone to write owner pages, service area pages and listing updates. A manager who bills owners for time may find it cheaper to hire help.

Hidden costs add up. Domain renewals, email, extra storage and premium templates appear on many builder pages. Wix lists storage by plan, from 2 GB on Light to 100 GB on Business. A listing-heavy site with many photos can pass a small cap, so check storage before you pick a tier.

What should you ask before you pick a property management website builder?

Ask five questions and write down the answers. Vendors change plans often, so a written answer beats the page you read today.

Run a test before you commit. Build the owner page and the listings page on a trial, then load both on a phone. If either takes more than a few seconds to edit, the site will go stale by next quarter.

How do you choose a property management website builder?

Choose a property management website builder with a three-check filter: fit, cost and setup effort. Run every option through all three before you pay.

Fit: does it serve owners and tenants on separate pages, and can you edit page titles, descriptions and URLs?

Cost: add the plan price, domain, storage and any per-unit fee, then compare the total with one month of management fees.

Setup effort: can you launch the owner and listings pages in a week, or do you need a developer?

A small manager under 50 units can start on WordPress.com or Wix, with a free Google Business Profile and a link to the tenant portal. A manager at 100 units or more should compare DoorLoop, Buildium and Rentvine, then keep a separate marketing site for owners. A growing company should plan the marketing site as an asset it owns.

Set a short launch plan before you buy. Week one, claim the Google Business Profile and pick the platform. Week two, write the owner page and the listings page. Week three, link the tenant portal and test on a phone. Review traffic and calls after a month.

What is the best website builder for property management?

No single builder wins for every manager. Wix, Squarespace and WordPress.com suit managers who want a stand-alone marketing site. DoorLoop, Buildium and Rentvine list sites inside their platforms. Choose by who owns the domain, how much you can edit and the total yearly cost.

How much does a property management website cost?

Stand-alone builders here run from $4 a month on WordPress.com Personal billed every 12 months to $39.77 on Wix Business paid yearly. DoorLoop starts at $2.50 per unit a month. Domains, storage and add-ons cost more, so total the full year.

Does property management software include a website?

Some does. DoorLoop marks a company website as included. Buildium lists a marketing website as a feature without showing which plan has it. Rentvine lists a site feature but publishes no site price. Confirm what you get in writing before you sign.

Should a property manager use a stand-alone builder or platform site?

Many managers use both. The platform site handles tenant tasks, and a stand-alone marketing site wins owners with original pages for each service area. That split avoids lock-in. Ask who owns the domain before you build on any platform, and keep a copy of every page you write.

Is Google Business Profile free for a property manager?

Google states that you can add or claim your business at no charge. It still takes work: accurate service areas, photos of managed properties and replies to every review. Google's paid ad products, such as Local Service Ads, are separate and carry their own costs.

What should a new property manager build first?

Claim a free Google Business Profile and launch a simple site with an owner page, a listings page and a link to the tenant portal. Add city pages and an owner inquiry form next. Choose management software before you pay for a premium site.
